scenes.title: Athena Visits Nausicaa's Dream
scenes.summary: While much-enduring Odysseus sleeps, worn down by sleep and weariness, Athena goes to the city of the Phaeacians. They once lived in Hypereia near the overweening Cyclopes, until godlike Nausithous led them away to Scheria, drove a wall around the city, built houses and temples, and divided the plowlands; now Alcinous rules, who knows counsels from the gods. Athena rushes like a breath of wind to the bed of Nausicaa, who sleeps between two handmaids with beauty from the Graces, and stands above her head in the likeness of the daughter of Dymas, famous for ships. She asks why her mother bore her so slack: her glossy clothes lie uncared for, her marriage is near, and the best men of the Phaeacians are courting her. She tells her to urge her father at dawn to make ready the mules and the wagon, and promises to go along as a fellow worker to the washing pools, a long way from the city. Then Athena goes away to Olympus, the seat of the gods that is never shaken by winds, wet by rain, or touched by snow.

scenes.title: Nausicaa Asks for the Carriage
scenes.summary: Dawn of the fair throne wakes Nausicaa, who wonders at the dream and goes through the house to tell her parents. Her mother sits at the hearth turning the sea-purple wool; her father is going out to the council of the famous kings. Nausicaa asks her papa dear for a high carriage with good wheels to take the soiled clothes to the river, saying that he should wear clean clothes in the council and that her five brothers always want freshly washed clothes for the dance. She feels shame to name her marriage, but he understands everything, grants the mules, and orders the slaves to make ready the carriage. Her mother packs food, relishes, wine in a goatskin, and olive oil in a golden flask, and Nausicaa takes the whip and the reins and drives off with her handmaids.

scenes.title: Washing and Play at the River
scenes.summary: At the never-failing washing pools by the river, the girls loose the mules to graze on the honey-sweet field grass, tread the clothes in the trenches in rivalry, and spread them out along the shore where the sea washes the pebbles clean. They bathe, anoint themselves, eat beside the banks, and then throw off their veils and play at ball while white-armed Nausicaa leads the song and dance. She stands out among her handmaids as Artemis of the showering arrows stands out among the nymphs on Taygetus or Erymanthus, and Leto is glad in her heart. When they are about to go home, Athena plans for Odysseus to wake and see the girl who will lead him to the city. The princess throws the ball toward a handmaid, misses, and throws it into a deep eddy; the girls shout aloud, and brilliant Odysseus wakes.

scenes.title: Odysseus Comes Out of the Thicket
scenes.summary: Sitting up, Odysseus wonders to what land of mortals he has come, whether they are arrogant and savage or kind to strangers and god-fearing, and whether the female cry he hears is of nymphs or of human beings who have speech. He decides to try for himself and see, breaks off a branch of leaves to shield his genitals, and comes out from the thickets like a mountain-bred lion, rained upon and blown by the wind, whose belly bids him go even into the close-built fold. Terrible he appears, marred by the brine, and the handmaids flee this way and that over the jutting beaches. Only the daughter of Alcinous stays, for Athena puts daring in her mind. Odysseus is torn two ways, whether to clasp her knees or to entreat her from a distance with soothing words, and chooses to stand apart, lest the girl be angry if he touches her knees.

scenes.title: Odysseus Supplicates Nausicaa
scenes.summary: Odysseus beseeches her as queen, asking whether she is a goddess or a mortal: if a goddess, he likens her most closely to Artemis; if a mortal, her father, lady mother, and brothers are thrice blessed, and most blessed is the man who leads her home with his bride-gifts. Awe holds him as it did on Delos, when he saw a young palm sapling springing up beside the altar of Apollo on the journey that brought him evil sorrows. Yesterday, on the twentieth day, he escaped the sea from Ogygia, and now a god has cast him here; he asks her to show him the town and give him a rag to throw around himself. He prays that the gods may give her a husband, a home, and like-mindedness, for nothing is better than a man and a woman who keep a house with one mind. Nausicaa answers that Zeus deals out prosperity to the good and the bad as he wishes, and that he must endure it. She promises him clothing and what befits a much-tried suppliant, and tells him that the Phaeacians hold this land and that she is the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous.

scenes.title: The Bath and Athena's Grace
scenes.summary: Nausicaa orders her handmaids to stand still: no hostile man comes to the land of the Phaeacians, who are dear to the immortals and live far apart in the much-surging sea, and all strangers and beggars are from Zeus. The handmaids sit Odysseus down in the shelter, lay out a cloak and a tunic, and give him oil in the golden flask, but he asks them to stand some way off, for he feels shame to strip naked among girls with lovely tresses. He washes the brine from his back and broad shoulders and the scurf of the sea from his head, and puts on the clothes. Athena makes him taller and sturdier and lets fall curling locks like the hyacinth flower, pouring grace upon him as a skilled man pours gold around silver. Nausicaa gazes at him and tells her white-armed handmaids that he now looks like the gods, and that she wishes such a man might be called her husband and stay here. The handmaids set food and drink beside Odysseus, and he eats greedily, for he has long been without food.

scenes.title: Nausicaa's Instructions
scenes.summary: Nausicaa folds the clothes, yokes the strong-hoofed mules, and climbs up, then tells Odysseus to rise and go to the city. Through the fields he is to walk with the handmaids behind the wagon, but before the city, with its high rampart, two harbors, ship-sheds, and assembly around the shrine of Poseidon, he must stay behind. She shuns the unkind talk of the overbearing men among the people, imagining some baser man who asks who this tall stranger is and whether she has found a husband from elsewhere because she dishonors the Phaeacians who woo her. He is to wait in the splendid poplar grove of Athena near the road, by her father's domain and orchard, until he expects that they have reached the house, then ask for the house of Alcinous, which even an infant could show him. Inside he is to pass by her father's throne and throw his hands around the knees of her mother, who sits at the hearth turning the sea-purple wool, for if she is minded in friendship toward him, he may hope to reach his native land. She lashes the mules and drives with judgment, so that the handmaids and Odysseus can follow on foot.

scenes.title: The Prayer in Athena's Grove
scenes.summary: The sun sets, and they come to the famous grove holy to Athena, where brilliant Odysseus sits down. He prays at once to the child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone: since she never listened when the famous shaker of the earth shattered him, she should listen now and grant that he may come to the Phaeacians as one dear to them and pitied. Pallas Athena hears him, but she does not yet appear to him face to face, for she stands in awe of her father's brother, who rages furiously against godlike Odysseus until he reaches his own land.

days.label: Night of Day 31
days.note: The night after Odysseus lands at the river mouth in Scheria (5.441–493), on the twentieth day after he left Ogygia (6.170). Odysseus sleeps under the olive bushes while Athena visits Nausicaa's dream.

days.label: Day 32
days.note: Dawn (6.48). Odysseus calls the day of his landing 'yesterday' (χθιζός, 6.170). The washing, the meeting at the river, and the drive toward the city fill the day; the sun sets at 6.321 at Athena's grove, and the same evening goes on in Book 7, where Odysseus enters the city and the house of Alcinous.
